analysis.one_liner: Requires cosmetics makers to register with the FDA, disclose every ingredient, prove safety, and pay oversight fees.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2010, the bill was referred to two House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overhauled federal oversight of cosmetics, which are currently regulated far more loosely than drugs or food. Companies that make, package, or distribute cosmetics would have to register annually with the FDA, disclose all ingredients on labels and websites (including fragrance components now kept secret as trade secrets), submit safety data to a public database, report serious adverse health effects, and pay fees scaled to their size. The FDA would build lists of banned, restricted, and proven-safe ingredients, gain authority to order recalls, and protect salon workers with expanded hazard sheets in English, Spanish, and Vietnamese. The bill never moved after being referred to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans who use cosmetics daily, especially vulnerable groups the bill named: pregnant women, infants, children, the elderly, and people with compromised immune systems. Salon and nail salon workers, who are exposed to professional products all day, would get expanded material safety data sheets available in multiple languages, and the public would get a searchable database of what is actually in the products they buy.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required annual registration of every establishment that manufactures, packages, or distributes cosmetics sold in the United States, including foreign ones, giving the FDA a complete picture of the industry for the first time.

It would have required full ingredient labeling on every package and on internet retail listings, and it specifically removed trade-secret protection from ingredients, including the components of fragrances, preservatives, and flavors.

The FDA would have been required to publish lists of prohibited, restricted, and proven-safe ingredients within two years, starting from authoritative hazard sources such as the EPA, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, and the National Toxicology Program, and to assess at least 300 ingredients within 18 months.

It would have created mandatory reporting of serious adverse health effects within 15 business days, with reports made publicly available with personal details redacted, and given the FDA authority to order a company to stop distributing or to recall a dangerous cosmetic.

It directed the Labor Department to issue a workplace safety standard requiring expanded material safety data sheets for professional-use cosmetics, available to salon owners and workers in English, Spanish, Vietnamese, and other languages on request.
Safety fees would only be assessed on companies with more than $1 million in annual gross receipts, prorated by size.
It required the FDA to favor non-animal testing methods where equivalent alternatives exist.

analysis.who_pays: Cosmetics and personal-care manufacturers, their ingredient and fragrance suppliers, and internet vendors, who would bear registration, testing, disclosure, and fee costs. Some of those compliance costs would likely be passed to consumers through prices, and ingredients lacking safety data could eventually be forced off the market.

drawbacks.text: The safety standard is extremely strict: an ingredient must be proven safe down to a one-in-a-million cancer or harm risk with a 1,000-fold uncertainty factor for vulnerable populations. Critics in the industry argued this bar, plus the rule that any ingredient with no safety determination within five years is banned from use, could sweep out large numbers of existing ingredients, including preservatives that keep products from spoiling.
Full fragrance and ingredient disclosure ends long-standing trade-secret protections, exposing proprietary formulations to competitors even though the bill keeps product concentrations confidential.

Even with the $1 million fee exemption, small cosmetics makers would face registration, labeling, safety-substantiation, and CEO-signed compliance statements, which is a real administrative burden for tiny brands even if the public benefit is real.

The bill placed large new duties on the FDA on fixed deadlines with no funding guarantee beyond an authorization to appropriate; an under-resourced agency could miss the deadlines, which under the bill would itself trigger market restrictions on affected ingredients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is substantial: Americans use these products daily, the existing federal framework barely requires pre-market safety proof, and the bill's worker-protection and disclosure provisions target real exposures. The costs are genuine but conventional regulatory compliance costs, concentrated on an industry that is overwhelmingly large companies, with the fee exemption cushioning small businesses. The bill's weakness is design, not intent: its one-in-a-million safety bar and five-year drop-dead rule for unassessed ingredients were unusually rigid and would have created real compliance strain, so the honest case against it is overreach, not pointlessness.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and it died quietly when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the Safe Cosmetics Act of 2010 on July 20, 2010, joined by Representatives Ed Markey and Tammy Baldwin as original sponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee.
That was the last action of any kind: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled in either committee.
Twenty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The bill expired on January 3, 2011, when the 111th Congress ended.
Versions of the idea resurfaced in later Congresses, and Congress eventually passed a narrower cosmetics modernization law in 2022, but this bill itself never advanced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cosmetics and fragrance makers came out ahead: they kept the existing light-touch regime, with no registration, no fees, no mandatory disclosure of fragrance ingredients, and no new safety-testing obligations. Consumers and salon workers got none of the promised protections.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 22 cosponsors was a House Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-run committees where it sat never brought it up.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed annual registration, CEO-signed safety certifications, recall authority, and prorated fees on companies with over $1 million in sales. Its death preserved the industry's lightly regulated status quo, where pre-market safety proof is not required.

The bill would have stripped trade-secret protection from fragrance, flavor, and preservative components and required them on labels and in a public database, ending one of the industry's most protected practices.

They were exempt from the fees, which applied only to companies above $1 million in annual receipts, but still faced registration, full ingredient labeling, and safety-substantiation requirements. Some small 'clean' brands would have gained a level playing field against large competitors.

industries.industry: Professional salon and nail salon operators
industries.note: Salon owners would bear new duties to keep expanded hazard sheets on hand, but the same provision directly protects their employees, who face the heaviest daily exposure to cosmetic chemicals.
